## Abstract

The Ring Loading Problem is an optimal routing problem arising in the planning of optical communication networks which use bidirectional SONET rings. In mathematical terms, it is an unsplittable multicommodity flow problem on undirected ring networks. We prove that any split routing solution to the Ring Loading Problem can be turned into an unsplittable solution while increasing the load on any edge of the ring by no more than $+\frac{19}{14}D$, where $D$ is the maximum demand value. This improves upon a classical result of Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler (1998) who obtained a slightly larger bound of $+\frac{3}{2}D$. We also present an improved lower bound of $\frac{11}{10}D$ (previously $\frac{101}{100}D$) on the best possible bound and disprove a famous long-standing conjecture of Schrijver et al. in this context.

...

Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler, in a landmark paper [12] (see also the annotated reprint [13]), present a clever analysis for a simple greedy algorithm that turns any split routing into an unsplittable routing while increasing the load on any edge by at most $\frac{3}{2}D$, where $D:=\max_{i,j}d_{i,j}$ is the maximum demand value. Their result thus implies $L\leq L^{*}+\frac{3}{2}D$. Khanna [8] shows how to use this bound in order to obtain a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the Ring Loading Problem. For the special case of uniform nonzero demands $d_{i,j}=D$, Schrijver et al. even prove $L\leq L^{*}+D$.

On the other hand, Schrijver et al. exhibit an instance of the Ring Loading Problem together with a carefully chosen split routing that cannot be turned into an unsplittable routing without increasing the load on some edge by at least $\frac{101}{100}D$. This observation, however, does not imply a gap strictly larger than $D$ between the optimum values of split and unsplittable routings. In the conclusion of their paper, Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler write:

> “…even though the mathematics refuses to cooperate, we guarantee $L\leq L^{*}+D$.”

...

Our main result is the following theorem.

**Theorem 1.**

Any split routing solution to the Ring Loading Problem can be turned into an unsplittable routing while increasing the load on any edge by no more than $\frac{19}{14}D$.

In particular, this result implies $L\leq L^{*}+\frac{19}{14}D$. Our algorithm runs in linear time and combines pairs of solutions obtained by the greedy algorithm of Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler [12] using a clean crossover operation. In the area of genetic algorithms, it is known that the additional use of crossover (also called ‘recombination’ or ‘sexual reproduction’) is empirically more effective than mutation only, and this can sometimes even be confirmed by theoretical evidence; see, e. g., [7, 6]. We are, however, not aware of previous approximation results relying on such crossover operations.

We also exhibit a relatively simple instance of the Ring Loading Problem together with particular split routings that cannot be turned into unsplittable routings without increasing the load on some edge by at least $\frac{11}{10}D$. After more than 15 years, our results are the first improvements on the classical results of Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler [12] (upper bound $\frac{3}{2}D$ and lower bound $\frac{101}{100}D$). Last but not least, we present an instance with $L=L^{*}+\frac{11}{10}D$, thus disproving Schrijver et al.’s long-standing conjecture $L\leq L^{*}+D$.

...

Schrijver et al. prove that $\beta\in[\frac{101}{100},\frac{3}{2}]$. As a consequence of our results, we narrow this interval down to $\beta\in[\frac{11}{10},\frac{19}{14}]$.

For an instance with $d_{i}\in\bigl[0,\frac{2}{7}D\bigr]\cup\bigl[\frac{5}{7}D,D\bigr]$ for every demand $i$, there is a pattern with additive performance at most $\frac{19}{14}D$.

## 5 Deriving an improved lower bound

In this section we present a counterexample to Schrijver et al.’s conjecture. While this counterexample turns out to be relatively simple and easy to verify, we would like to emphasize that finding it was a cumbersome undertaking for both the author and his computer. Schrijver et al. write in their paper [12] “We have never managed to produce a random example with $L>L^{*}+D$…”, and we can certainly confirm this experience. Among hundreds of millions of similar instances of the same size, all featuring a very special, promising structure, the one presented below turned out to be the only counterexample.

In the following we first give some more details on how we tracked down this shy beast. In fact, our primary objective was to find a split routing that cannot be turned into an unsplittable routing without increasing the load on some edge by $(1+\varepsilon)D$ for $\varepsilon>0$ as large as possible. Only later we realized that our insights can also be used to disprove Schrijver et al.’s conjecture.

Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler [12] exhibit an instance of the Ring Loading Problem on a ring of $n=26$ nodes and $m=13$ nonzero demands together with a split routing that cannot be turned into an unsplittable routing without increasing the load on some edge by at least $\frac{101}{100}D$. An illustration of a slightly simplified version of this instance with $n=24$ nodes and $m=12$ demands can be found in Figure 8.

For $m=8$ and $D=10$, there exist more than one billion such sequences $(u_{1},v_{1}),\dots,(u_{8},v_{8})$. Taking certain symmetries into account, this number can be reduced to several hundreds of millions. By brute force enumeration, we found exactly two split routings that cannot be turned into unsplittable routings without increasing the load on some edge by at least $11=D+1$: the one depicted in Figure 2 and the one depicted in Figure 9.

There exist instances with a given split routing such that in any unsplittable solution the load on some edge is increased by at least $\frac{11}{10}D$ (cf. Figures 2 and 9).

This observation does, however, not yet imply the existence of a counterexample to Schrijver et al.’s conjecture. Firstly, the split routings in Figures 2 and 9 are not optimum (notice that an optimum split routing for pairwise crossing demands splits every demand into two equal pieces). And, secondly, it is not true that any unsplittable routing increases the maximum edge load by more than $D$.

This careful modification of the considered instances almost solves the second problem as well. As a consequence of Observation 4, any unsplittable routing increases the maximum edge load by at least $\frac{11}{10}D$ as long as it sticks to routing the additional demands along their corresponding edges. The latter restriction, however, turns out to be crucial. The instance depicted in Figure 10 (based on Figure 2) has an unsplittable routing whose maximum edge load exceeds the maximum edge load of the optimum split routing by only $D=10$.

On the other hand, the extension of the instance depicted in Figure 9 does lead to a counterexample, a slightly simplified version of which is depicted in Figure 11.

Figure 11: An instance of the ring loading problem on $n=16$ nodes with $18$ demands, $8$ of which belong to opposite nodes, $4$ to neighboring nodes, and $6$ to nodes of distance $2$.

...

Similar to above, it is easy to see that combining the split routing in Figure 9 with the straightforward ‘short’ routing of the additional demands yields an optimum split routing where all edge loads are equal to $L^{*}=39$. Finally, by enumerating all $2^{18}=262.144$ unsplittable routings, one can verify that the optimal unsplittable load is $L=50$ such that $L=L^{*}+D+1$, thus disproving Schrijver et al.’s conjecture that $L\leq L^{*}+D$.

## 6 Conclusion

We have shown that the worst-case additive gap between optimum split and unsplittable routings for the Ring Loading Problem is at most $+\frac{19}{14}D$ and at least $+\frac{11}{10}D$. That is, $L\leq L^{*}+\frac{19}{14}D$ for all instances, and there exists an instance with $L\geq L^{*}+\frac{11}{10}D$. Our extensive yet unsuccessful search for instances yielding a larger lower bound gives us serious doubts as to whether there exist any.

**Conjecture 1.**

$L\leq L^{*}+\frac{11}{10}D$ for all instances of the Ring Loading Problem.

We have serious doubts as to whether the algorithmic techniques and analytic tools discussed in this paper are powerful enough to close the remaining gap. But we hope that, 16 years after the publication of Schrijver et al.’s landmark paper [12], the presented progress will stimulate further research and new ideas on this fine and challenging problem.

highlights:
The following problem arose in the planning of optical communications networks which use bidirectional SONET rings. Traffic demands d i,j are given for each pair of nodes in an n-node ring; each demand must be routed one of the two possible ways around the ring. exa_hits.title: An Improved Upper Bound for the Ring Loading Problem
highlights:
## Abstract

The ring loading problem emerged in the 1990s to model an important special case of telecommunication networks (synchronous optical network rings) which gained attention from practitioners and theorists alike. Given an undirected cycle on $n$ nodes together with nonnegative demands between any pair of nodes, the ring loading problem asks for an unsplittable routing of the demands such that the maximum cumulated demand on any edge is minimized. Let $L$ be the value of such a solution. In the relaxed version of the problem, each demand can be split into two parts where the first part is routed clockwise while the second part is routed counterclockwise. Denote with $L^*$ the maximum load of a minimum split routing solution. In a landmark paper, Schrijver, Seymour, and Winkler [ SIAM J. Discrete Math., 11 (1998), pp. 1--14] showed that $L \leq L^* + \frac{3}{2}D$, where $D$ is the maximum demand value. They also found (implicitly) an instance of the ring loading problem with $L = L^* + \frac{101}{100}D$. Recently, Skutella [ SIAM J. Discrete Math., 30 (2016), pp. 327--342] improved these bounds by showing that $L \leq L^* + \frac{19}{14}D$, and there exists an instance with $L = L^* + \frac{11}{10}D$. We contribute to this line of research by showing that $L \leq L^* + \frac{13}{10}D$. We also take a first step toward lower and upper bounds for small instances.

exa_hits.title: Some aspects of graph sparsification in theory and practice
highlights: Many applications in transportation, telecommunication, logistics, biology or social networks, only to name a few examples, can be modelled by graphs. The size of graphs encountered in these applications is large, ranging from millions of vertices and edges in the European road network to billions of vertices and one hundred billion edges in the World-Wide Web graph. The order of magnitude of these graphs makes even the simplest queries infeasible. Summarizing, graphs are everywhere and graphs are large. These two simple observations lead to the important research area of graph sparsification that is heavily studied by practitioners and theorists alike. At the core, the objective of graph sparsification is simple, find a smaller representation of a graph that maintains important properties. The smaller graph has the advantage that queries can be answered faster and the memory requirement is reduced. In general, there is a trade-off between the size of the smaller graph and the 'quality' of the maintained property. In this thesis, we will show on a variety of problems that graph sparsification can be useful in multiple ways. We first investigate a theoretic model that allows graph sparsification using edge contractions while shortest path distances are approximately preserved. We show in this context some special cases where optimal contractions can be computed in polynomial time, that the problem is NP-hard in general, and deduce some results on asymptotic bounds on the size of the smaller graph. As a second problem, we analyse a warehouse location problem originating from logistics incorporating many constraints from practice where the main task is to connect customers to open facilities. Our approach contracts subsets of customers into meta-customers on different levels of granularity, allowing for a fine control on instance size and solution quality. The third considered problem is the ring loading problem, a variant of unsplittable multicommodity flows where demands between pairs of vertices are routed in a ring network such that the edge load of the ring is minimized. Schrijver, Seymour and Winkler showed in this context that the sparsification of the demands reveal nice structural properties. As a result, we use the properties of the sparsifications to improve upon the best known bounds on the edge loads. In the fourth problem, we seek as many orthogonal chain decompositions of the n-dimensional hypercube as possible. One crucial observation is the usage of the necklace poset as smaller representation of the cube. Only this sparsification technique allows us to find multiple such structures using a computer search.

highlights:
The Ring Loading Problem emerged in the 1990s to model an important special case of telecommunication networks (SONET rings) which gained attention from practitioners and theorists alike. Given an undirected cycle on $n$ nodes together with non-negative demands between any pair of nodes, the Ring Loading Problem asks for an unsplittable routing of the demands such that the maximum cumulated demand on any edge is minimized. Let $L$ be the value of such a solution. In the relaxed version of the problem, each demand can be split into two parts where the first part is routed clockwise while the second part is routed counter-clockwise. Denote with $L^{*}$ the maximum load of a minimum split routing solution. In a landmark paper, Schrijver, Seymour and Winkler [MR1612841] showed that $L\leq L^{*}+1.5D$, where $D$ is the maximum demand value. They also found (implicitly) an instance of the Ring Loading Problem with $L=L^{*}+1.01D$. Recently, Skutella [MR3463048] improved these bounds by showing that $L\leq L^{*}+\frac{19}{14}D$, and there exists an instance with $L=L^{*}+1.1D$. We contribute to this line of research by showing that $L\leq L^{*}+1.3D$. We also take a first step towards lower and upper bounds for small instances.

...

Given an undirected cycle on $n$ nodes together with non-negative demands between any pair of nodes, the Ring Loading Problem asks for an unsplittable routing of the demands such that the maximum cumulated demand on any edge is minimal. Formally, we are given a graph $G=\left(V,E\right)$ with nodes $V=\left[n\right]:=\left\{1,\ldots,n\right\}$, edges $\left\{i,i+1\right\}$ for each $i\in V$, where we assume throughout the paper that $\left\{n,n+1\right\}:=\left\{n,1\right\}$, and demands for each pair of nodes $i<j$ of value $d_{i,j}\geq 0$. By a slight abuse of notation, we refer to both the demand from $i$ to $j$ and its value as $d_{i,j}$. An unsplittable solution decides for each demand whether it should be routed clockwise, sending all of its value along the path $\left\{i,i+1,\ldots,j\right\}$, or counter-clockwise, sending all of its value along the path $\left\{i,i-1,\ldots,1,n,\ldots,j\right\}$. The load of an edge, for a given solution, is the sum of all demand values that are routed on paths that use the edge. We call the maximum load on any edge of the ring the load of the solution. The problem is to find an unsplittable routing that minimizes the load.

highlights:
$C_{1d}$ is the largest constant for which one has \(\max_{t \in \mathbb{R}} \left|\int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t-x) f(x)\ dx\right| \geq C_{1d} \left(\int_{-1/4}^{1/4} f(x)\ dx\right)^2\) for all real-valued (not necessarily non-negative) $f \colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ supported on $[-1/4,1/4]$.

This is the maximum of $\lvert f*f \rvert$ over $t$, for signed $f$. It is not the quantity $\lvert \max_t f*f \rvert$, whose records are smaller and which is a different constant; the two are sometimes conflated.

exa_hits.title: autocorr-3 — hillclimb
highlights:
Construct a step function f on [-1/4, 1/4], positive and negative values allowed, given as K = 400 equal-width bins (width h = 1/(2K) = 0.00125), that makes

C3(f) = max over t of |(f f)(t)| / (∫ f)^2, (f f)(t) = ∫ f(t - x) f(x) dx

as small as possible. This is the constant of the third autocorrelation inequality (Appendix B.3 of arXiv:2506.13131). Every f with ∫ f != 0 proves `C3 <= C3(f)`. Since f may change sign, cancellations in f*f can push the peak below what any non-negative f achieves (C3 <= C1). The best known value is 1.4557 (AlphaEvolve 2025, a 400-bin step function on this same grid), improving 1.4581 (Vinuesa 2010).

###### Abstract.

We show that there does not exist a constant $c<1$ such that $\lVert f\ast f\rVert_{\textup{L}^{2}}^{2}\leqslant c\,\lVert f\ast f\rVert_{\textup{L}^{1}}\lVert f\ast f\rVert_{\textup{L}^{\infty}}$ holds for every nonnegative $f\in\textup{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R})\cap\textup{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R})$.

...

For every nonzero nonnegative $f\in\textup{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R})\cap\textup{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R})$, set

$\mathfrak{R}(f):=\frac{\lVert f\ast f\rVert_{\textup{L}^{2}}^{2}}{\lVert f\ast f\rVert_{\textup{L}^{1}}\lVert f\ast f\rVert_{\textup{L}^{\infty}}}.$

Let $c$ be the supremum of the ratios $\mathfrak{R}(f)$ over all such $f$. Clearly, $c\leqslant 1$. Martin and O’Bryant [14, Conj. 4.4] conjectured that the optimal upper bound for these ratios over probability densities supported on $[-1/4,1/4]$ was $(\log 16)/\pi$. They restated the conjecture in [15, Conj. 2.9] and formulated it for all nonnegative functions in $\textup{L}^{1}(\mathbb{R})\cap\textup{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R})$ in [16, Conj. 5.2]. Matolcsi and Vinuesa [17] disproved the proposed bound. The value of $c$ remained open and was subsequently discussed by O’Bryant [19] and by Barnard and Steinerberger [1, §1.4].

highlights: How can we use AI to discover a new state of the art for a scientific problem? Prior work in test-time scaling, such as AlphaEvolve, performs search by prompting a frozen LLM. We perform reinforcement learning at test time, so the LLM can continue to train, but now with experience specific to the test problem. Our solutions are reviewed by experts or the organizers. All our results are achieved with an open model, OpenAI gpt-oss-120b, and can be reproduced with our publicly available code, in contrast to previous best results that required closed frontier models. ### D.12 Third Autocorrelation Inequality

The third autocorrelation inequality extends the first one to functions that take values of either sign: for every function $f$ supported on $[-\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{4}]$,

$\displaystyle\max_{-1/2\leq t\leq 1/2}\lvert(f\ast f)(t)\rvert\geq C_{3}\left(\int_{-1/4}^{1/4}f(x)\,dx\right)^{2},$

(22)

where $(f\ast f)(t)=\int f(t-x)f(x)\,dx$ is the autoconvolution of $f$. Every such $f$ with a nonzero integral gives an upper bound on $C_{3}$. Find a function $f$ supported on $[-\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{4}]$, with values of either sign and a nonzero integral, that minimizes this bound,

$\displaystyle\min_{f}\;\frac{\max_{t}\lvert(f\ast f)(t)\rvert}{\left(\int f\right)^{2}}.$

(23)

The program represents $f$ by its values $f_{1},\dots,f_{N}$ on $N$ equal intervals of $[-\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{4}]$ and chooses $N$.

#### Evaluator.

The entry function run() returns $f_{1},\dots,f_{N}$, the bound $\tilde{v}$, a loss value, and $N$. With the interval width $\Delta=1/(2N)$, the evaluator computes

$\displaystyle v=\frac{\max_{k}\Delta\left\lvert\sum_{i}f_{i}f_{k-i}\right\rvert}{\left(\Delta\sum_{i}f_{i}\right)^{2}}.$

(24)

The autoconvolution of a step function is piecewise linear with breakpoints at multiples of $\Delta$, so $v$ is the exact bound of the step function with values $f_{i}$. The evaluator requires $(\Delta\sum_{i}f_{i})^{2}\geq 10^{-9}$ and $\lvert v-\tilde{v}\rvert\leq 10^{-3}$, and the score uses $\tilde{v}$. The evaluator divides by 1.4557, AlphaEvolve’s bound on $\lvert\max_{t}(f\ast f)(t)\rvert/(\int f)^{2}$; for $v$ as defined here, AlphaEvolve’s value is $v_{\mathrm{AE}}=1.4688$.

With Qwen3 8B and 32B-FP8, SwarmEvolve improves on AlphaEvolve on the same three problems: it matches the best known packing of 26 circles in the unit square [62], and its step functions improve AlphaEvolve’s bounds on the second and third autocorrelation inequalities. The three baselines improve on AlphaEvolve only on the autocorrelation inequalities.

Two problems need care in the comparison with AlphaEvolve. On the third autocorrelation inequality, the evaluator of OpenEvolve takes the absolute value of the autoconvolution inside the maximum, while AlphaEvolve’s published bound of 1.4557 takes it outside the maximum. Under the definition of the evaluator, AlphaEvolve’s construction gives 1.4688, the value that we compare against (Appendix D.12). On the uncertainty inequality, the evaluator accepts only functions built from Hermite polynomials. Within this family, AlphaEvolve’s first construction gives 0.3521, while its best bound of 0.3216 uses Laguerre polynomials, which lie outside the family. SwarmEvolve reaches 0.3521 with Qwen3 32B-FP8, the value of AlphaEvolve’s construction within the same family.

## What was found

As part of a sweep across open problems in mathematical analysis, AlphaEvolve improved the upper bound on the Erdős minimum-overlap constant from about 0.380927 to about 0.380924, the first movement since 2016, and improved constants in autocorrelation inequalities. The gains are numerically small but exceed long-standing records, and the constructions are explicit and checkable.

...

The minimum-overlap constant and the autocorrelation inequalities have well-tracked records. AlphaEvolve's values were compared against the standing bounds and confirmed to improve them.

Caveats and known objections

The improvements are marginal in magnitude, and both were improved again by other automated systems in 2026. As with the other AlphaEvolve results, a human-designed evaluator and search loop did the selecting.
